title: The Blue Rope
paragraphs: From the jetty, the sea at Kampung Teluk Batu had looked like a sheet of hammered tin, flat and harmless. Nadia had taken three photographs of it before breakfast. Now, an hour out in her uncle’s boat, with the village shrunk to a line of rust-coloured roofs, she understood that the sea was not something one looked at. It was something one was on, and it did not care whether she was comfortable.

Pak Long stood at the stern under the one patched sail, with a bare foot on the tiller, steering as casually as other people scratch an itch. He had said perhaps twenty words to her since she arrived from Singapore four days ago, most of them “Eat”. Her mother called him stubborn. Watching him haul in the first net hand over hand, Nadia thought the word was too small.

It was she who saw the cloud first, though she did not know what she was seeing. Far to the east the sky had turned the purple-grey of an old bruise, and under it the water had lost its shine. “Pak Long,” she said, “is that rain?” He glanced over his shoulder for no longer than a breath. Then he looked at the net still in the water, at the few fish already silver in the hold, and at her. She watched him weigh the three.
“We go back,” he said. He began pulling in the net, half empty, fast. He did not sound afraid, and that frightened her more than shouting would have.

The wind arrived before the rain did, and every wave it touched stood up white. The boat, which had rocked like a cradle all morning, began to buck. Spray hit Nadia’s face, warm and salty. Her phone was in her pocket; for once it did not occur to her to take it out. She gripped the wooden bench until her knuckles hurt, and stared at the back of her uncle’s faded shirt as if it were the only steady thing in the world.

“Nadia.” He had to say it twice. “The blue rope. Hold. When I say, you let go — not before.” He pointed with his chin. She crawled to it on her knees. The rope was wet and rough and alive, tugging like a dog that has seen a cat, and she wrapped it twice around her fist the way she had seen him do. She was shaking. She held on anyway.

The rain came down all at once, as though someone had slit a bag. She could no longer see the roofs. She could barely see her uncle. But she could hear him, and when at last he shouted “Now!” she opened her hand. Something heavy swung across above her head, and the boat, which had been fighting the waves, turned and began to run with them.

Twenty minutes later they bumped against the jetty. Her aunt was waiting under a sheet of plastic with a towel, scolding them both before the boat was even tied. Pak Long said nothing. He lifted the single basket of fish onto the planks, then reached down and pulled Nadia up after it with one hard, wet hand.

He did not let go at once. He turned her palm over. The rope had left two red stripes across it. He looked at them for a moment, nodded once, and went to see to his boat. Nadia closed her hand around the stripes, as carefully as if they were something she had been given.

questions.text: In Paragraph 1, the village had ‘shrunk to a line of rust-coloured roofs’. What does the word ‘shrunk’ tell you about where the boat was?

scheme.answer: The boat had gone so far out to sea that the village looked tiny in the distance.
accept: They were a long way from the shore.

seeds.text: The boat was so far out at sea that the village looked very small.
They had travelled a long way from the shore, so the houses seemed tiny.
The village was a very small one with only a few houses.
The village had become smaller because people were moving away.
It tells us the boat was on the sea.

questions.text: In your own words, explain how Nadia’s idea of the sea changed once she was out on the boat (Paragraph 1).

scheme.answer: From the shore she had thought of it as a calm, safe thing to admire [1]; out on it, she saw that it was a powerful place she was at the mercy of, with no concern for her [1].
points: Before: a calm / safe / pretty sight to admire from land.
Now: something powerful that she was in the middle of and at the mercy of — it had no concern for her.

seeds.text: At first she thought the sea was just a calm and safe thing to admire from the land. Out on the boat she realised it was powerful and had no concern for her, and she was at its mercy.
Before, it was only a pretty view to her that could do no damage. Now she was in the middle of it and saw that she was at its mercy.
On the boat she realised the sea was powerful and she was at its mercy.
At first she thought the sea was just a calm, safe view to admire.
The sea had looked flat and harmless. Now she understood that the sea was not something one looked at. It was something one was on, and it did not care whether she was comfortable.
She used to be afraid of the sea but now she found it beautiful and took photographs.

scheme.answer: He was deciding whether to stay and bring in a full catch, which was his living [1], or to head back at once to keep his niece safe from the storm [1].
points: On one side: staying to finish fishing / the catch (his income).
On the other: Nadia’s safety — getting her home before the storm.

scheme.answer: Any two of the three details, 1 mark each.

questions.text: In Paragraph 5, the boat ‘had rocked like a cradle all morning’ but then ‘began to buck’. What does each of these descriptions suggest about the movement of the boat?

scheme.answer: ‘Rocked like a cradle’ suggests a gentle, soothing, safe motion [1]; ‘buck’ suggests violent jerking, like an animal trying to throw off its rider [1].
points: ‘Buck’: sudden, violent jerking, as if trying to throw them off — dangerous.

seeds.text: 'Rocked like a cradle' suggests the boat was swaying gently and felt safe. 'Buck' suggests it was jerking violently like an animal trying to throw them off.

At first the boat moved gently and it was comforting, like for a baby.
'Buck' shows the boat was jumping about violently like a wild horse.

They suggest that the boat was moving in different ways.
